newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rival Israeli MPs draft joint peace guideline.
newsitem.headline: Rival Israeli MPs draft joint peace guideline.

text.p: Some members of Israel's ruling Likud party and the main opposition Labour party on Sunday took the unprecedented step of agreeing on joint principles for final peace talks with the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had reservations about the document. He said it was the result of a private initiative and was not binding on the government.
Key to the document -- drafted by Likud parliamentary faction head Michael Eitan and Labour's Yossi Beilin and signed by them and six other legislators -- were the following clauses:
"The majority of settlers will live on their settlements under Israeli sovereignty, in order to preserve territorial continuity between the settlements and the State of Israel.

"The residents of the Israeli settlements that will exist outside of the area that will be annexed by the State of Israel will receive special, agreed upon arrangements" preserving their Israeli citizenship and ties to Israel.
More than 130,000 Jewish settlers live amidst some two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

Beilin said Labour members agreeing publicly to any annexation of West Bank territory and to settlements remaining was "a very big change", as was the Likud side's agreeing some settlements would be on territory ruled by Palestinians.
"It would be possible to lead the opposition towards support of the government if it goes this way," Beilin said.

Eitan said: "It will be a platform not only for political, external negotiations with the Palestinians but also for peace among the Jews in Israel." He said he hoped it would influence the government which is soon to begin final status peace talks.

Netanyahu's office said: "The document presented by parliament members from the Likud and Labour is the fruit of a private initiative...and it does not obligate the government nor the prime minister...the prime minister has reservations over different sections of the document."
Beilin is a candidate in elections for Labour party leader due in June. Ehud Barak, front-runner in the race to lead Labour, was not involved in the initiative. Barak was not available to comment.

The document said the establishment of a "Palestinian entity" with "limits on...sovereignty" would have to be permitted. Eitan, sticking to his party's line, described the entity as expanded autonomy. Beilin said he envisioned a state.

On Jerusalem, the eastern half of which was seized by Israel in 1967 and is claimed by Palestinians, the document said: "Israel will recognise the governing centre of the Palestinian entity which will be within the borders of the entity and outside the existing municipal borders of Jerusalem."

That leaves open a solution mooted some time ago in Israeli media reports in which Palestinians would rule from the Arab East Jerusalem neighbourhood of Abu Dis which does not formally fall within the Israeli-drawn boundaries of Jerusalem.
Asked how Palestinians -- who demand an independent state with East Jerusalem as capital and an end to settlements -- could accept any deal on such principles, Beilin said:
"Reality is stronger than all of us. If the Palestinians want to have a Palestinian state...they have to pay a price too."

Israel has handed most of the Gaza Strip and eight major towns in the West Bank to Palestinian rule since a landmark interim peace deal in September 1993. Final peace talks, which have yet to begin, are to conclude by May 1999.
